data.name: Light_Brightness_Title
data.value: How bright is a lamp?

data.name: Light_Brightness_P1
data.value: A lamp turns electricity into light. Double its power and twice as much light lands on the floor, yet the floor does not look twice as bright. Try it: the first few watts make a big difference, the last few hardly any.

data.name: Light_Brightness_P2

data.name: Light_Brightness_Deeper

data.name: Light_Tilt_P1

data.name: Light_Shadow_Title
data.value: Sharp and soft shadows

data.name: Light_Shadow_P1
data.value: A lamp hangs over a box. Stand anywhere on the floor and ask: how much of the lamp can I see past the box? Where it is all hidden, the shadow is full; where only part of it is hidden, the shadow is part dark.

data.name: Light_Shadow_P2
data.value: A small lamp is hidden all at once, so its shadow has a sharp edge. A big lamp, or a cloudy sky, is hidden a little at a time, so the edge fades gently. Raise the lamp, grow it, move it aside, and watch the edge.

data.name: Light_Shadow_Deeper
data.value: The fully dark part is the umbra, the soft edge the penumbra. The picture works out, for every point of the floor, how much of the lamp it can see.

data.name: Light_Radiance_Title
data.value: Why a wall looks as bright from far away

data.name: Light_Radiance_P1
data.value: Walk away from a lit wall and it does not get dimmer. Odd, since each bit of it now sends you less light. But each speck of your eye now takes in more of the wall: twice as far, four times as much wall, each part a quarter as bright to you.

data.name: Light_Radiance_P2
data.value: Turn the panel away and the same thing happens: the eye takes in more of it, and a matte surface sends less light off at a slant, by just as much. What stays the same is how bright the surface looks — its radiance — which is what eyes and cameras measure.

data.name: Light_Radiance_Deeper
data.value: Area seen ∝ distance² / cos, light from each bit ∝ cos / distance²: the product is 1. A surface that holds this at every angle is called Lambertian.

data.name: Light_Bounce_Title
data.value: Colour, and light that bounces

data.name: Light_Bounce_P1
data.value: A red wall is red because it gives back mostly red light and keeps the rest. White gives back all colours. With no bounces, only what the lamp reaches is lit, and the box's shadow side is pitch black.

data.name: Light_Bounce_P2
data.value: Add a bounce: everything lit now lights everything else. The floor near the wall turns faintly red, and shadows fill in. A second and third bounce add less each time. This is why rooms are never as dark in the shade as the lamp alone would make them.

data.name: Light_Bounce_Deeper
data.value: Each bounce passes light between every pair of points: how much one sends, times how squarely the two face each other, over the distance squared. Computer graphics calls this radiosity, or global illumination.

data.name: Gears_Ratio_Title
data.value: Wheels that turn each other

data.name: Gears_Ratio_P1
data.value: Press two wheels together and turn one: the other turns the opposite way. Where they touch, both rims move the same distance, so the small wheel has to spin round more times to keep up with the big one.

data.name: Gears_Ratio_P2

data.name: Gears_Ratio_Deeper

data.name: Gears_Torque_Title
data.value: Slower, but stronger

data.name: Gears_Torque_P1
data.value: Gears cannot make something out of nothing. When a small gear drives a big one, the big gear turns slower, and in return it turns harder. The teeth push on each other equally hard, but the big gear feels that push further from its centre, like a longer spanner.

data.name: Gears_Torque_P2
data.value: That is how a hand crank lifts a heavy load: a small gear turns a big drum gear, trading speed for force. Run it the other way round and you trade force for speed, which is what a bicycle does when its big front sprocket spins the small back one fast.

data.name: Gears_Torque_Deeper
data.value: Turning force (torque) = push × distance from the centre. With 3 times as many teeth, the drum turns 3 times slower and 3 times harder: speed × turning force stays the same, apart from what friction takes.

data.name: Gears_Involute_Title
data.value: The shape of a tooth

data.name: Gears_Involute_P1
data.value: Wind a string round a can, tie a pencil to its end and unwind it, keeping the string tight. The pencil draws a curve that spirals away from the can. Good gear teeth have exactly this curve on both sides. It is called an involute.

data.name: Gears_Involute_P2
data.value: Why that curve? The tight string always meets the curve at a right angle. So when two such teeth press on each other, the push always runs along one straight line, at one angle, however far the gears have turned. The gears turn smoothly, without tugging or rattling.

data.name: Gears_Involute_Deeper
data.value: The can is the gear's base circle. The string that has come off is as long as the arc of the can it came off, so the pencil moves away steadily as you unwind.

data.name: Gears_Mesh_Title

data.name: Gears_Mesh_P1
data.value: Watch the gold dots: they mark where teeth are touching. Each one slides along the same slanted line, from where a pair of teeth first meet to where they let go. Before one pair lets go, the next pair has already met, so the push never stops.

data.name: Gears_Mesh_P2

data.name: Gears_Mesh_Deeper
data.value: The line of action touches both base circles. It crosses the line between the centres at the pitch point, where the two rolling circles meet, and the push between the teeth always points along it.

data.name: Watch_Spring_Title
data.value: Stored up in a spring

data.name: Watch_Spring_P1
data.value: A mechanical watch has no battery. Its energy is a long, thin strip of steel, the mainspring, coiled up inside a little drum called the barrel. Turning the crown winds the spring tight round the arbor in the middle.

data.name: Watch_Spring_P2
data.value: Left alone, the spring tries to uncoil and pushes the barrel round. The barrel has teeth on its rim, and they drive all the other wheels. A full spring keeps a watch like this one going for about 40 hours.

data.name: Watch_Spring_Deeper
data.value: The spring pulls hardest when it is full and less as it runs down. On its own that would make the watch run fast, then slow; the part on the next pages that lets the energy out a little at a time is what keeps the rate steady.

data.name: Watch_Hands_P1
data.value: Between the barrel and the hands is a row of wheels, the going train. Each big wheel drives a small pinion on the next axle, so each axle turns faster than the one before. The centre wheel turns once an hour and carries the minute hand; the fourth wheel turns once a minute and carries the seconds hand.

data.name: Watch_Hands_P2

data.name: Watch_Hands_Deeper

data.name: Watch_Escape_P1
data.value: Left to itself, the spring would whirl the wheels round and run down in seconds. The escapement stops that. A lever with two red stones holds the escape wheel still; each time the balance swings past the middle, it flicks the lever across, one stone lets go, the wheel jumps half a tooth, and the other stone catches it. That jump is the tick you hear.

data.name: Watch_Escape_P2
data.value: The wheel does not just get let go: as it slips past a stone, its tooth gives the lever a small push, and the lever passes it on to the balance. That push, once a beat, keeps the balance swinging for as long as the spring lasts.

data.name: Watch_Escape_Deeper
data.value: Two beats per tooth, 15 teeth per turn, 10 turns a minute: 300 beats a minute, 18,000 an hour. The balance is free for most of each swing and touches the lever only near the middle, which is why this kind is called a detached lever escapement.

data.name: Watch_Balance_P1
data.value: What sets the pace is the balance: a little wheel on a hair-thin spiral spring. Turn it and the spring pulls it back; it overshoots, the spring pulls the other way, and it swings to and fro like a swing in a playground, two and a half times a second.

data.name: Watch_Balance_P2
data.value: The trick is that a wide swing and a narrow swing take the same time: a wider swing just moves faster. So as the spring runs down and the pushes get weaker, the watch keeps its rate. A stiffer hairspring, though, speeds it up, and a few tenths of a percent is minutes a day.

data.name: Watch_Balance_Deeper
data.value: Swings a second = √(spring stiffness ÷ heaviness of the wheel) ÷ 2π. The swing's width is not in it. Watchmakers adjust the rate by changing how much of the hairspring is free to bend.

data.name: Watch_Rotor_Deeper

data.name: Bicycle_Wheel_Title
data.value: Standing on wires

data.name: Bicycle_Wheel_P1
data.value: A bicycle wheel looks too flimsy to carry anyone: a thin rim held to the hub by a few dozen wires no thicker than a knitting needle. A wire is no good at pushing (it just bends), but it is very good at pulling. So the wheel is built with every spoke already pulled tight, like the strings of a guitar.

data.name: Bicycle_Wheel_P2
data.value: When you sit on the bike, your weight presses the hub down towards the road. The spokes under the hub, where the rim is squeezed a little against the ground, lose some of their pull; the rest hardly change. All the spokes pulling round the hub no longer balance, and the difference holds you up. As the wheel rolls, each spoke takes its turn at the bottom.

data.name: Bicycle_Wheel_Deeper
data.value: Build the spokes too loose and a heavy load takes away all the pull of the ones underneath: they go slack, nothing holds the rim there, and the wheel can buckle. The pull lost by the spoke straight below is only about a fifth of the load; the spokes beside it share the rest.

data.name: Bicycle_Chain_Title
data.value: From your feet to the wheel

data.name: Bicycle_Chain_P1
data.value: The pedals turn a big toothed wheel, the chainring. A chain wraps round it and round a small sprocket on the back wheel. Each link of the chain sits in a gap between two teeth, so the chain cannot slip: however many teeth the chainring turns past, the sprocket turns past just as many.

data.name: Bicycle_Chain_P2
data.value: So if the chainring has twice as many teeth as the sprocket, the back wheel turns twice for every turn of the pedals. That is how a bike outruns a runner: your legs go round slowly, the wheel spins quickly, and each turn of the wheel rolls you about two metres.

data.name: Bicycle_Chain_Deeper
data.value: Wheel turns per pedal turn = chainring teeth ÷ sprocket teeth. Times the wheel's roll (about 2.1 m for a road bike), that is how far each pedal turn takes you. A chain link is half an inch (12.7 mm) long, the same on almost every bike in the world.

data.name: Bicycle_Hill_Title
data.value: Gears for hills

data.name: Bicycle_Hill_P1
data.value: Legs are happiest at one rhythm, about eighty turns of the pedals a minute, and they can only push so hard for long. On the flat, a big gear (a small sprocket at the back) turns that rhythm into a good speed. Up a hill, the same gear would need a push no one can keep up.

data.name: Bicycle_Hill_P2
data.value: So the back wheel carries a stack of sprockets, and a derailleur lifts the chain from one to the next. On a bigger sprocket each pedal turn takes you less far, so the same rhythm carries you more slowly, but every push gets lighter by just as much. You climb slowly, but you climb.

data.name: Bicycle_Hill_Deeper
data.value: Going up, most of your effort lifts you and the bike: on an 8% road, every 100 m along also climbs 8 m. The work for a whole climb is much the same in any gear; the gear only decides whether you do it with many light pushes or a few heavy ones.

data.name: Bicycle_Freewheel_Title
data.value: Coasting

data.name: Bicycle_Freewheel_P1
data.value: On a toy tricycle the pedals are fixed to the wheel: when the wheel turns, your feet have to go round too. A bicycle lets you stop pedalling and roll on. The trick is hidden in the back hub, and you can hear it: that ticking as you coast.

data.name: Bicycle_Freewheel_P2
data.value: The sprocket turns an inner part, the driver, which carries two small pawls pressed outwards by springs. The wheel's shell around it has teeth on the inside, like a saw. Pedal forwards and the pawls catch a tooth and drag the wheel round. When the wheel runs faster than the pedals, the teeth slide under the pawls instead, lifting them and letting them snap down again: tick, tick, tick.

data.name: Bicycle_Brakes_Title
data.value: Stopping

data.name: Bicycle_Brakes_P1
data.value: Brakes squeeze pads against the rim, or against a disc on the hub. The rubbing turns your speed into heat; after a long downhill the rims can be too hot to touch. Stopping takes more room than you might think: at twice the speed you need four times as far, because there is four times as much energy of motion to turn into heat.

data.name: Bicycle_Brakes_P2
data.value: When you brake, your body wants to keep going, so your weight tips forwards onto the front wheel and off the back one. A tyre can only grip the road as hard as it is pressed onto it, so the front brake can stop you far harder than the back one, whose wheel soon skids. Too hard on the front, though, and the back wheel lifts.

data.name: Bicycle_Brakes_Deeper
data.value: How much weight moves onto the front wheel depends on how high the centre of mass sits compared with the wheelbase. Here it is as high as the wheelbase is long, with 40% of the weight on the front: past about 0.6 g, all of it is on the front and the bike tips over. A car is long and low, so it can brake much harder without tipping.

data.name: Bicycle_Steer_Title
data.value: Why it steers itself straight

data.name: Bicycle_Steer_P1
data.value: Push a bike along by its saddle and tilt it a little: the handlebars turn by themselves, into the lean, and the bike straightens up. Much of that comes from the shape of the front end. The fork turns about a tilted line, the steering axis, and that line meets the ground a little in front of where the tyre touches it.

data.name: Bicycle_Steer_P2
data.value: That gap is called the trail. It works like the little wheels of a shopping trolley, which trail behind their pivots: whenever the wheel is knocked sideways, the road drags its touch point back behind the pivot, and the wheel lines up straight again. Without trail the wheel does not come back; with the touch point in front, it swings right away.

data.name: Bicycle_Steer_Deeper
data.value: Trail = (wheel radius × cos head angle − fork offset) ÷ sin head angle. Road bikes have about 55–65 mm: less makes the steering light and nervous, more makes it heavy and slow to turn. Trail is only part of the story: the spinning wheels and where the weight sits help too, and riders keep their balance mostly by steering a little towards the side they are falling.

data.name: Boats_Float_Title

data.name: Boats_Float_P1
data.value: Lower a wooden block into water and it pushes some of the water out of the way. The water pushes back, upwards, and the deeper the block goes, the more water it has pushed aside and the harder the water pushes. The block stops sinking when that push matches its weight.

data.name: Boats_Float_P2
data.value: And how hard is that push? Exactly the weight of the water pushed aside. A block half as heavy as the same amount of water floats half under; ice, nearly as heavy as water, floats almost all under. Something heavier than its own size of water can never push aside enough, and sinks.

data.name: Boats_Float_Deeper

data.name: Boats_Pressure_Title

data.name: Boats_Pressure_P1
data.value: Water has weight, so the water at the bottom of a pool is squeezed by all the water above it. That squeeze is pressure, and it presses on anything in the water from every side. Every metre deeper adds about a tenth of the air's own pressure: dive to ten metres and your ears feel it.

data.name: Boats_Pressure_P2
data.value: Hold a cube under water. The water presses on its sides too, but those pushes cancel out. The bottom is deeper than the top, so it is pressed harder; the water pushes up on the bottom more than it pushes down on the top. That difference is the water's push upwards, and it is the same however deep the cube goes.

data.name: Boats_Pressure_Deeper
data.value: Pressure = water's density × gravity × depth. The difference between bottom and top is density × gravity × the cube's height; times the area of a face, that is density × gravity × the cube's volume: the weight of the water it pushes aside, just as the last spread said.

data.name: Boats_Stability_Title
data.value: Steady or top-heavy

data.name: Boats_Stability_P1
data.value: Whether a boat rights itself depends on a race. As it tips, the water's push slides to the low side; but the higher the boat's weight sits, the further its centre swings out to the low side too. If the weight's centre swings out further than the push, the pair tips the boat further instead, and over it goes.

data.name: Boats_Stability_P2
data.value: So heavy things go low: engines and fuel deep in the hull, sometimes tonnes of extra weight, called ballast, at the very bottom. A wider boat helps too, because tipping it moves its push much further. Stacking cargo high on deck, or crowding everyone to the top, can turn a steady boat into one that rolls over.

data.name: Boats_Stability_Deeper
data.value: For small tips, the water's push seems to come from a fixed point above the boat, the metacentre. Its height above the centre of weight, GM, sums it up: positive and the boat rights itself (bigger is stiffer); negative and it will not stay upright. For a box-shaped boat, the metacentre is width² ÷ (12 × draft) above the middle of the water pushed aside.

data.name: Boats_Submarine_P1
data.value: A submarine is built a little lighter than the water it pushes aside when fully under, so with nothing else to do, it floats. To dive, it opens valves and lets the sea into its ballast tanks. It gets no bigger, but it gets heavier, and once it is heavier than its own size of water, it sinks.

data.name: Boats_Submarine_P2
data.value: To come up again it blows the water out of the tanks with compressed air, and it is light once more. In between is a narrow balance: exactly as heavy as its water, it hangs where it is. But only just: a few litres either way and it slowly drifts up or down, so crews keep trimming the tanks and steer with fins like a fish.

data.name: Boats_Submarine_Deeper
data.value: Unlike a boat, a submarine under water has no waterline to settle at: the water's push no longer grows as it goes deeper, so nothing brings it back to one depth. Fish have the same problem and solve it with a swim bladder, a bag of gas they fill or empty a little.

data.name: Car_Crank_Title
data.value: From up-and-down to round and round

data.name: Car_Crank_P1
data.value: In an engine, burning fuel pushes a piston down a cylinder. But wheels need turning, not pushing. The answer is the oldest trick in machinery: a crank, an arm on the shaft with a pin near its edge, joined to the piston by a connecting rod. Push the piston down and the crank swings round; the crank's momentum then brings the piston back up again.

data.name: Car_Crank_P2
data.value: The piston does not follow a neat wave. When the crank is near the top, the rod tilts as the pin swings sideways, which adds to the piston's drop; near the bottom the tilt takes some back. So the piston hurries through the top half of its travel and dawdles through the bottom half, and it moves fastest a little before the crank is sideways. The shorter the rod, the more lopsided this gets.

data.name: Car_Crank_Deeper
data.value: Travel from the top = r + l − (r cos θ + √(l² − r² sin² θ)), for a crank of radius r and a rod of length l turned θ from the top. With an endlessly long rod this would be the plain wave r(1 − cos θ). Car engines use rods about three to four times the crank's radius: long enough to keep the rod from pushing the piston hard against the cylinder's side, short enough to keep the engine compact.

data.name: Car_Cam_Title
data.value: Opening on time

data.name: Car_Cam_P1
data.value: Each cylinder breathes through valves: one lets fresh air and fuel in, another lets the burnt gas out. They must open and close at exactly the right moments, thousands of times a minute. A camshaft does it. A cam is a wheel with a bump; as it turns, the bump presses the valve open against a strong spring, and as it passes, the spring snaps the valve shut.

data.name: Car_Cam_P2
data.value: An engine takes two turns of the crank to work through its cycle, and each valve opens once in that time. So the camshaft is geared, or chained, to turn once for every two turns of the crank. The cam's shape decides everything: how far the valve opens, and for how long. Engines built for high speed use cams that hold the valves open longer.

data.name: Car_Cam_Deeper
data.value: At 3,000 turns a minute the crank turns 50 times a second, so a valve open for 240° of crank turn is open for about 13 thousandths of a second. The spring must be stiff enough to keep the valve following the cam's fall; too soft, and at high speed the valve floats and is late to close.

data.name: Car_Cylinders_Title
data.value: Smooth turning

data.name: Car_Cylinders_P1
data.value: A single cylinder pushes on the crank for only half a turn in every two; for the rest of the cycle it pushes nothing, or even takes a little back to squeeze the next charge. On its own it would jerk the car forward in pulses. A flywheel, a heavy disc on the crankshaft, stores energy during the push and gives it back in between, keeping the crank turning.

data.name: Car_Cylinders_P2
data.value: More cylinders take turns, so the pushes overlap and fill the gaps. With four cylinders there is always one pushing; with six or eight, the turning force is nearly steady. That is why bigger engines run so smoothly, and why a single-cylinder lawnmower needs a heavy flywheel.

data.name: Car_Cylinders_Deeper
data.value: The crank speeds up while the turning force is above its average and slows while it is below. The energy it gains and loses over a cycle, over the flywheel's own stored energy (½ × its inertia × speed²), gives the size of the wobble: twice the flywheel, half the wobble.

data.name: Car_Clutch_Title
data.value: Moving off

data.name: Car_Clutch_P1
data.value: An engine cannot turn slower than a certain speed or it stalls, yet the car starts from standing still. Something has to join a spinning engine to still wheels gently. That is the clutch: a disc with a grippy lining, squeezed by strong springs between the engine's flywheel and a pressure plate.

data.name: Car_Clutch_P2
data.value: Press the pedal and the pressure plate is pulled back: the disc spins free and nothing is passed on. Let the pedal up slowly and the springs squeeze harder and harder; the plates slip, rubbing, and the gearbox side speeds up while the engine labours. Once both turn at the same speed, they grip and turn as one.

data.name: Car_Clutch_Deeper
data.value: While the plates slip, the energy the engine puts in is partly lost as heat: the turning force passed × the difference in speed. That is why riding the clutch wears it out, and why it can smell hot after a hill start. Once it grips, no energy is lost there at all.

data.value: Round a bend

data.name: Car_Bend_P1
data.value: On a bend, the outer wheels go round a bigger circle than the inner ones, so they have further to roll in the same time. If the two driven wheels were fixed to one axle, one of them would have to scrub along the road, wearing the tyre and fighting the steering.

data.name: Car_Bend_P2
data.value: The differential solves it. The engine turns its case through the big ring gear; inside, small spider gears ride round with the case and mesh with a side gear for each wheel. Going straight, the spiders do not spin and both wheels turn with the case. On a bend, the spiders spin, letting one wheel turn faster and the other slower, while the case turns at their average.

data.name: Car_Bend_Deeper
data.value: Left wheel turns + right wheel turns = 2 × case turns, always. On a bend of radius R, with the wheels a track t apart, the outer wheel rolls (R + t/2) for every (R − t/2) of the inner. On a tight 5 m turn with a 1.6 m track, that is about 38% more.

data.name: Car_Ice_P1
data.value: The differential has a catch. It always shares the turning force equally between the two wheels. That is fine while both grip; but put one wheel on ice, and it can take only a little force before it spins. Since the other wheel gets the same, it gets only a little too: the icy wheel spins madly and the car hardly moves.

data.name: Car_Ice_P2

data.value: With an open differential, the push the car gets is at most twice what the slippier wheel can take. Locked, it is what both can take together. A locked differential fights the car on a dry bend, though, so it is unlocked again once off the ice.

data.name: Locks_Pins_Title
data.value: Pins at the shear line

data.name: Locks_Pins_P1
data.value: Most front-door locks are pin-tumbler locks. Inside a fixed shell sits a plug, a brass cylinder that the key turns. Above the keyway a row of holes runs up through the plug and into the shell, and in each hole stands a little stack: a key pin at the bottom, a driver pin on top of it, and a spring pressing both down. With no key in, every driver pin is pushed partway into the plug, and the plug cannot turn.

data.name: Locks_Pins_P2
data.value: The plug and the shell meet along a thin gap called the shear line. Push the right key in and each cut lifts its key pin by exactly the right amount, so the top of every key pin stops on the shear line and every driver pin sits wholly in the shell. Nothing crosses the gap, and the plug turns. A cut a little too shallow lifts its pin too far; a little too deep, not far enough. Either way a pin bridges the gap.

data.name: Locks_Pins_Deeper
data.value: In this lock each step of cut is half a millimetre, and a pin must stop within about a twentieth of a millimetre of the line. Real locks are made to about that accuracy too, which is why a copied key cut slightly wrong can feel gritty, or not turn at all. The key pins are all different lengths, each matched to its cut; the driver pins are all alike.

data.name: Locks_Keys_Title
data.value: How many different keys?

data.name: Locks_Keys_P1
data.value: A key is really just a list of numbers: how deep each cut goes. If a cut can take ten depths and a key has five cuts, there are ten choices for the first, ten for the second, and so on: ten times ten times ten times ten times ten, a hundred thousand keys. One more cut multiplies that by ten again.

data.name: Locks_Keys_P2
data.value: Not all of them can be made. If one cut is very shallow and the next very deep, the slope between them is so steep that a pin cannot slide over it as the key goes in, and the key would jam or snap. So makers set a largest step allowed between neighbouring cuts. That throws out many combinations, and the real count is smaller than the simple product.

data.name: Locks_Keys_Deeper
data.value: Counting the allowed keys is a neat puzzle: go cut by cut, and for each depth keep a tally of how many keys could end there. The next cut's tally for a depth is the sum of the tallies of every depth close enough to it. A hundred thousand keys sounds like plenty, but a building with many doors also needs master keys, which use some of them up.

data.name: Locks_Master_P1
data.value: In an office or a hotel, each door has its own key, but the caretaker carries a single master key that opens them all. The trick is a thin extra pin, a master wafer, slipped between key pin and driver pin wherever the two keys differ. Now that stack can part in two places: at the top of the key pin, or at the top of the wafer.

data.name: Locks_Master_P2
data.value: The shallower of the two cuts lifts the key pin's top to the shear line. The deeper cut lets the stack sit lower by exactly the wafer's thickness, so the wafer's top lands on the line instead. Either key opens the door. But there is a catch: a key that takes some cuts from one and the rest from the other works too, though nobody ever cut it.

data.name: Locks_Master_Deeper
data.value: With wafers in three of the five stacks, each of those three has two working depths, so 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 different keys open this lock. In a big building, several levels of master keys mean more wafers and more keys that work by accident. Careful planning of the cuts, and keys that are hard to copy, keep the risk down.

data.name: Locks_Binding_P1
data.value: If every hole in a lock were drilled in exactly the same line, turning the plug gently would press on all the pins at once, and none could move. But no machine is perfect. The holes wander by a few hundredths of a millimetre, so when the plug is turned a hair, the hole furthest out of line pinches its pin first, and only that one.

data.name: Locks_Binding_P2
data.value: Push that pin up until the join between its two pins reaches the shear line, and its driver is caught on the edge of the plug. The plug turns a fraction more, and now the next hole out of line pinches its pin. Pin by pin, a lock can be opened without its key. Good locks fight back with very precise holes, and with oddly shaped driver pins that catch in the wrong place.

data.name: Locks_Binding_Deeper
data.value: This is why a lock's security depends so much on how precisely it is made, not only on how many keys it allows. Designers add spool- or saw-toothed driver pins, extra side bars, and pins that must also be turned to the right angle. Each adds a test that the key passes easily and a tool does not.

data.name: Locks_Lever_P1
data.value: Long before pin tumblers, and still on many back doors and safes, there is the lever lock. Its bolt carries a small post, the stump. Over the bolt lie flat levers, each with a window the stump sits in and, running from the window, a narrow channel called the gate. While the stump is in the windows, the levers hold the bolt still.

data.name: Locks_Lever_P2
data.value: The key's bit has steps of different heights, one for each lever. As the key turns, each step lifts its lever, and for a moment every gate is level with the stump. Just then the bit catches the bolt and slides it along, the stump running through the gates. Lift one lever too little or too much, and the stump meets solid metal.

data.name: Locks_Lever_Deeper
data.value: More levers allow more keys and make the lock harder to cheat: good door locks have five or more. Some levers have false notches cut beside the gate, so a probing tool catches in the wrong place. The idea is the same as with pins: the bolt moves only when several separate parts all agree.

data.value: A combination padlock has no keyhole. Each numbered wheel turns on a sleeve with a notch in it, and a bar lies along the sleeves, holding the shackle down. Only when every wheel shows its number are all the notches at the top, in a row; then the bar drops into them, and the shackle springs free.

data.name: Locks_Dials_P2
data.value: Three wheels of ten numbers give a thousand settings, so on average a stranger would need five hundred tries. But cheap wheels are made loosely, with notches wider than they should be. Then the numbers either side of the right one work too, and each try covers several settings at once. A loose lock can be far weaker than its numbers suggest.

data.name: Locks_Dials_Deeper

Better locks keep their notches tight and add false ones, so a wheel that seems to give a little on a wrong number gives nothing away. A safe's single dial drives its wheels one after another with pins, but the notches and the bar work the same way.

data.value: A lever is the simplest machine of all: a stiff bar that turns about a pivot. Put a heavy stone on one end and press on the other. If the pivot stands nearer the stone, the stone's side of the bar is short and yours is long, and a small push on the long side holds up a heavy load on the short one.

data.name: Lifting_Seesaw_P2
data.value: There is a price. As the bar turns, the long end sweeps through a bigger arc than the short end. If your arm is four times as long as the stone's, you push with a quarter of the force, but your hand has to travel four times as far. The work you do, force times distance, is the same as the work done on the stone: a lever trades force for distance, it never makes work out of nothing.

data.name: Lifting_Seesaw_Deeper
data.value: Your push times the length of your arm equals the load times the length of its arm: that balance is the law of the lever. Scissors, a bottle opener, a wheelbarrow and the bones of your forearm are all levers. A wheelbarrow puts the pivot at one end and the load in the middle; your forearm does the opposite, giving away force so that your hand can move fast.

data.name: Lifting_Pulley_Title
data.value: One wheel, one rope

data.name: Lifting_Pulley_P1
data.value: A pulley is a wheel with a groove for a rope. Hang one from a beam, put the rope over it, tie a bucket to one end and pull the other. Pulling down is easier than lifting up, because you can lean your weight on the rope, but you still pull exactly as hard as the bucket weighs, and the bucket rises exactly as far as you pull. A fixed pulley only turns the force round.

data.name: Lifting_Pulley_P2
data.value: Now hang the pulley on the bucket instead. Tie one end of the rope to the beam, run it down under the wheel and back up to your hand. The bucket now hangs from two strands, and each carries half its weight, so you pull with half the force. But to lift the bucket one metre, both strands must get a metre shorter, so two metres of rope pass through your hands.

data.name: Lifting_Pulley_Deeper
data.value: A rope pulls equally along its whole length when the wheel turns freely, so each strand that holds the load carries the same share of it. Count the strands holding the load and you have the ratio: one strand, no gain; two strands, half the force and twice the rope. Cranes and sailing boats use both kinds: moving pulleys to multiply force, fixed ones to lead the rope to where someone can pull it.

data.name: Lifting_Tackle_P1
data.value: Join several pulleys and you get a block and tackle: a fixed block of wheels at the top, a moving block at the bottom, and a single rope wound back and forth between them. Each run of rope between the blocks is a strand, and every strand helps to hold the load. With four strands, each carries a quarter of the engine, and you pull with a quarter of its weight.

data.name: Lifting_Tackle_P2
data.value: As before, you pay in rope. For the engine to rise one metre, all four strands must each get a metre shorter, so four metres of rope pass through your hands. Real wheels also rub on their axles: each wheel the rope runs round keeps back a little of the pull, so with many strands you pull a bit harder than the simple count says.

data.name: Lifting_Tackle_Deeper
data.value: In this picture the wheels are drawn side by side so that every strand shows; in a real block they sit on one axle, one behind another. If each wheel passes on 95 percent of the pull, four strands give not four times the force but about three and a half times. With many wheels the losses add up, which is why big cranes use wheels that turn on ball bearings.

data.name: Lifting_Winch_Title
data.value: Crank, drum and worm

data.name: Lifting_Winch_P1
data.value: A winch is a lever that never runs out of room. The rope winds onto a small drum, and you turn the drum with a crank. Your hand goes round a big circle while the rope winds round a small one: with a crank six times as long as the drum's radius, you hold the load with a sixth of its weight, and you can keep turning for as long as there is rope.

data.name: Lifting_Winch_P2
data.value: Let go of the crank, though, and nothing stops the load from falling and spinning the handle round. A worm fixes this: a screw that turns a toothed wheel on the drum, one tooth for each turn of the screw. It multiplies your force many times over and, because its thread slopes so gently, the load cannot turn it backwards. The load stays wherever you leave it.

data.name: Lifting_Winch_Deeper
data.value: A worm holds its load because of friction: the thread slopes so gently that pushing on it from the wheel's side only presses it harder against the teeth. The same friction costs you something: in this winch more than half of your work turns into heat in the thread. Wasted effort in return for a load that holds itself: that is why worms turn up in winches, gates and the tuning pegs of guitars.

data.name: Lifting_Jack_Title
data.value: Pushing with oil

data.name: Lifting_Jack_P1
data.value: A hydraulic jack lifts a car with a pump and some oil. Oil hardly squeezes at all, and when you push on it, the pressure spreads equally through all of it. The pump is a narrow piston; the ram that lifts the car is a wide one. The same pressure pushes on every square centimetre of both, so a ram with sixteen times the area gets sixteen times the force.

data.name: Lifting_Jack_P2
data.value: Again, you pay in distance. The oil the narrow pump pushes out spreads under the wide ram in a thin layer, so each stroke lifts the car only a little. Two ball valves make the pumping work: one lets oil from the tank into the pump as you raise the handle, the other lets it out to the ram as you press down, and neither lets it flow back.

data.name: Lifting_Jack_Deeper
data.value: With the ram four times as wide as the pump, its face has sixteen times the area; the handle is another lever, six to one. Together they let a press of about ten kilograms hold up a thousand. To lower the car, a release screw opens a path from the ram back to the tank. A car's brakes work the same way: a narrow piston under the pedal, wide ones at the wheels.

data.name: Lifting_Elevator_Title
data.value: The lift and its counterweight

data.name: Lifting_Elevator_P1
data.value: A lift car hangs from steel ropes that run over a grooved wheel at the top of the shaft, turned by a motor. If the ropes held nothing else, the motor would have to hold the whole car and everyone in it, and lift all of that every time the car went up.

data.name: Lifting_Elevator_P2
data.value: So the other ends of the ropes carry a counterweight, as heavy as the empty car plus about half a full load. Now the motor only holds the difference between the two sides. With the car half full they balance, and whether it is empty or full, the difference is never much more than half a load. Going up full or coming down empty, the counterweight does most of the work.

data.name: Lifting_Elevator_Deeper
data.value: In most lifts the motor does not wind the ropes up at all: they simply lie over the wheel and are gripped by friction in its grooves. In this lift that grip holds as long as one side is not more than about two and a half times as heavy as the other, and the counterweight makes sure of it. If either side comes to rest on the buffers at the bottom of the shaft, the ropes go slack, slip on the wheel, and nothing more is dragged upward.

data.name: Plumbing_Tower_Title
data.value: Height is pressure

data.name: Plumbing_Tower_P1
data.value: Water is heavy: a bucket of it is hard to carry. Pile water up and the bottom layers carry the weight of everything above them, so the deeper you go, the harder the water pushes. Every ten metres of depth adds about one bar, roughly the push of the whole atmosphere on top of us.

data.name: Plumbing_Tower_P2
data.value: A water tower uses this. It holds a tank of water high above the town, joined by pipes to every house. The pressure at a tap depends only on how far the tower's water stands above it, not on the shape or length of the pipes on the way. A tap on the ground floor gets plenty; a tap near the top of a tall building gets little, and one higher than the tower's water gets none at all.

data.name: Plumbing_Tower_Deeper
data.value: Water joined by pipes settles at one level, wherever it is: pour water into a garden hose bent into a U and both ends fill to the same height. That is why the dashed line matters. Tall buildings that rise above their town's water pressure keep pumps in the basement and tanks on the roof, so their own tank can feed the top floors from just above them. Many towns pump water up into towers at night, when electricity is cheap, and let it flow down all day.

data.name: Plumbing_Tap_Title
data.value: Inside a tap

data.name: Plumbing_Tap_P1
data.value: Under the handle of an old-style tap is a screw. Turning the handle winds a rod, the spindle, up or down through a threaded hole. On the spindle's end sits a rubber washer, and below the washer is a round hole, the seat, with water under pressure waiting beneath it.

data.name: Plumbing_Tap_P2
data.value: Screwed down, the washer presses on the seat and the water cannot pass. Turn the handle and the washer lifts a little; water squeezes through the ring-shaped gap between them, round the washer and out of the spout. The thread turns a big movement of your hand into a tiny, precise lift, and holds the washer down against the water's push.

data.name: Plumbing_Tap_Deeper
data.value: The gap the water passes through is a ring: the seat's rim times the lift. Once the lift reaches a quarter of the seat's width, that ring is as big as the hole itself, and lifting further changes nothing; that is why the first turn or two matter and the rest do not. A dripping tap usually has a hardened or torn washer that no longer seals. Many newer taps use two ceramic discs with holes instead, which line up as you turn a lever a quarter of a turn.

data.name: Plumbing_Siphon_Title
data.value: Water that climbs

data.name: Plumbing_Siphon_P1
data.value: A siphon empties a tank over its rim without a pump. Fill a hose with water, put one end in the tank and lead the other over the edge and down, lower than the tank's water. The water in the hose runs out of the low end, and more climbs up into the hose behind it, over the crest, for as long as the end stays low.

data.name: Plumbing_Siphon_P2
data.value: Nothing in the hose pulls. The air presses on the tank's water and pushes it up the short leg; at the low end, the water's weight in the long leg wins. The two sides of the crest are like two weights on a rope over a pulley: the longer column falls and drags the shorter one up. Raise the end above the tank's water and the balance turns, and the flow stops.

data.name: Plumbing_Siphon_Deeper
data.value: The faster flow comes from a bigger drop: from the tank's surface down to the hose's end, not from the height of the crest. But the crest cannot be too high. Above about ten metres the air cannot push water up any further: the pressure at the top falls so low that the water there boils into vapour even when it is cold, and the column breaks. A hose full of air does nothing, which is why a siphon has to be filled before it starts.

data.name: Plumbing_Cistern_Title
data.value: The float that turns itself off

data.name: Plumbing_Cistern_P1
data.value: Behind a toilet is a tank that fills itself, then stops, with nobody watching. The water comes in through a valve at the top. On the valve is an arm, and on the end of the arm a hollow float that rides on the water.

data.name: Plumbing_Cistern_P2
data.value: While the water is low, the float hangs down and the arm holds the valve open. As the tank fills, the float rises and tips the arm, which pushes the valve slowly shut. At the level it is set for, the valve closes and the water stops. Flush, and the water rushes out through a flap in the floor; the float drops, the valve opens, and the whole thing starts again.

data.name: Plumbing_Cistern_Deeper
data.value: This is feedback: the result of the filling, the water's level, works the valve that does the filling. The nearer the water gets to its mark, the less the valve lets in, so it slows as it arrives instead of overshooting. The overflow pipe is there in case the valve fails or is set too high: the water then runs away down the pipe instead of over the floor. The same idea, a measurement steering the thing that changes it, runs a room's thermostat and a car's cruise control.

data.name: Plumbing_Trap_Title
data.value: The bend under the sink

data.name: Plumbing_Trap_P1
data.value: Look under a sink and the pipe does not go straight down: it dips into a U and comes up again before it joins the drain. Water always stays in the bottom of that U. It is a plug of water between your room and the drain, which is full of smelly air, and it stops that air coming up through the plughole.

data.name: Plumbing_Trap_P2
data.value: The water stands up to the lip where the bend spills into the drain. The part of it above the bend's lowest top edge is the seal, a few centimetres deep. Each time you use the sink, fresh water pushes the old water over the lip, and the seal is renewed. As long as it stays deeper than zero, no bubble of drain air can get past.

data.name: Plumbing_Trap_Deeper
data.value: When a toilet flushes further along the same drain, its rush of water drags the air behind it and lowers the pressure in the pipe. That suction pulls the sink side of the seal down; the drain side cannot rise to match, because it just spills away. If the suction is as deep as the seal, the trap is sucked empty and you hear it gurgle. That is why drains have vent pipes running up through the roof: they let outside air into the drain, so the suction never builds.

data.name: Plumbing_Pump_Title
data.value: Why a pump cannot suck

data.name: Plumbing_Pump_P1
data.value: An old hand pump stands on top of a well. Lifting its handle draws a piston up a cylinder, and water follows the piston up the pipe from the well. It looks as if the pump sucks the water up. It does not: the piston only takes air away from above the water in the pipe.

data.name: Plumbing_Pump_P2
data.value: What lifts the water is the air pressing on the well's surface outside the pipe. With less air pushing down inside the pipe, the outside air pushes water up it. Two ball valves keep each lift from slipping back. But the air can only push so hard: it balances a column of water about 10.3 metres tall. If the well's water is deeper than that, the water stops in the pipe, however hard you pump.

data.name: Plumbing_Pump_Deeper
data.value: Real pumps manage less, about seven or eight metres, because their seals leak a little and because water near the top of the column, at very low pressure, starts to boil into bubbles. Deep wells therefore put the pump down at the water: a long rod from the handle works it, or an electric pump sits under water. A pump down there pushes the water up from below, and pushing has no such limit. The same ten metres limits a siphon. It puzzled pump makers four hundred years ago, and explaining it led to the discovery that air has weight.

data.name: Bridges_Beam_Title
data.value: A plank across a stream

data.name: Bridges_Beam_P1
data.value: The simplest bridge is a plank resting on two banks. Stand in the middle and it bends a little. As it bends, its upper side gets shorter, squeezed, and its lower side gets longer, stretched. It is the wood's resistance to being squeezed and stretched that holds you up.

data.name: Bridges_Beam_P2
data.value: Length makes a beam bend far more than you might guess: twice as long, and the same load makes it sag eight times as much. Depth works just as strongly the other way: a plank twice as deep sags only an eighth as much. So a longer bridge needs a much deeper beam, and soon the beam gets too heavy to carry even itself.

data.name: Bridges_Beam_Deeper
data.value: The middle of a beam's depth is neither squeezed nor stretched; the work is done near the top and the bottom faces. That is why steel beams are made in the shape of an I: two wide flanges far apart, joined by a thin web, with little metal in the middle where it would do nothing. For the same reason floor joists stand on their narrow edge. The wood is the same; turning it on edge makes it many times stiffer.

data.name: Bridges_Frame_Title
data.value: Why triangles

data.name: Bridges_Frame_P1
data.value: Join four bars into a square with a pin at each corner, so each corner can turn. Push the top sideways and the square folds over into a slanting shape. None of the bars got longer or shorter; the corners simply turned. A square has no way of holding its shape.

data.name: Bridges_Frame_P2
data.value: Add one bar across a diagonal and the square becomes two triangles. Now it will not fold at all, because a triangle cannot change its shape unless one of its sides changes length. Push it, and the brace is stretched instead. A bar is very strong along its length, so a few triangles of thin bars can be both light and stiff.

data.name: Bridges_Frame_Deeper
data.value: The brace here carries more than the push: about one and four-tenths times as much, because it leans at forty-five degrees and only part of its pull acts sideways. Push from the other side and the same brace would be squeezed instead, which is why many frames have braces both ways, or one stout enough to take either. Look for triangles in cranes, roof timbers, electricity pylons and bicycle frames.

data.name: Bridges_Truss_Title
data.value: The truss

data.name: Bridges_Truss_P1
data.value: A truss is a deep beam with most of it left out: a row of triangles made of straight members. When a lorry drives onto it, the whole truss bends a little, just like a plank. Its top members, the top chord, are squeezed; its bottom members, the bottom chord, are stretched.

data.name: Bridges_Truss_P2
data.value: The diagonals between them carry the load across, from panel to panel, out to the banks. Each member is only squeezed or stretched along its length, never bent, and a straight bar is far stronger that way. A taller truss works like a deeper beam: twice as tall, and its chords carry half the force.

data.name: Bridges_Truss_Deeper
data.value: These forces are not guessed: at every joint the members' pulls and pushes must balance the load on it, and together those balances fix every force exactly. That is how the picture works them out. Move the lorry and watch the diagonals swap: one that was squeezed may become stretched. Steel is good at both, but long squeezed members can buckle sideways, so they are usually made thicker than the stretched ones.

data.name: Bridges_Arch_Title
data.value: The arch

data.name: Bridges_Arch_P1
data.value: Stone is strong when it is squeezed and weak when it is stretched, so a long stone beam cracks along its stretched underside. An arch avoids stretching altogether. Its wedge-shaped stones lean on each other, and their weight presses each one against its neighbours, all the way down to the ground.

data.name: Bridges_Arch_P2
data.value: But an arch does not only push down: it also pushes outward on the banks, trying to spread its feet. That outward push is the thrust, and solid ground or heavy blocks called abutments must hold it. The flatter the arch, the harder it pushes outward; a tall, round arch pushes outward much less.

data.name: Bridges_Arch_Deeper
data.value: While an arch is being built its stones cannot stand on their own, so they are laid on a temporary wooden frame. The keystone at the top goes in last; only then does the ring hold itself, and the frame can be taken away. Lean on any one stone of a finished arch and you only squeeze it harder. Many stone arch bridges built two thousand years ago are still carrying traffic.

data.name: Bridges_Cable_Title
data.value: Hanging from a cable

data.name: Bridges_Cable_P1
data.value: A suspension bridge turns the arch upside down. Instead of stones squeezed together, it hangs its deck from steel cables that are only ever stretched. The main cables drape between two tall towers, hangers drop from them to the deck, and their ends run back down to huge anchor blocks set in the ground.

data.name: Bridges_Cable_P2
data.value: The cable has to sag. The flatter it hangs, the harder it must pull to hold the same deck: half the sag, twice the pull. That pull runs along the cable to the tower tops and down the back stays into the anchors, which must hold it, just as an arch's abutments hold its thrust.

data.name: Bridges_Cable_Deeper
data.value: A cable carrying weight spread evenly along a deck hangs in a parabola, the same curve an arch takes upside down. A cable cannot buckle however long it is, while a long squeezed member can, which is why the longest bridges hang from cables. Their main cables are spun on site from thousands of thin wires laid side by side, then squeezed into a round bundle.

data.name: Bridges_Expansion_Title
data.value: Room to grow

data.name: Bridges_Expansion_P1
data.value: Steel grows as it warms. Not by much: a metre of it gets about a hundredth of a millimetre longer for every degree. But a bridge deck is hundreds of metres long, and between a winter night and a summer afternoon it can warm by fifty degrees, enough for a four-hundred-metre deck to grow and shrink by about a quarter of a metre.

data.name: Bridges_Expansion_P2
data.value: So the deck is pinned at one end only and rests on rollers or sliding bearings everywhere else. At the free end is an expansion joint: steel fingers on the deck slide between fingers on the abutment, leaving a gap that opens in the cold and closes in the heat, while wheels roll smoothly across.

data.name: Bridges_Expansion_Deeper
data.value: Held fast at both ends, the deck could not grow, and it would push on the abutments with thousands of tonnes, enough to crack them or make the deck buckle upward. Railway lines meet the same problem; long welded rails are stretched when they are laid, so that on hot days they are squeezed far less. You can hear expansion joints as a regular thump-thump when a car drives across a long bridge.

data.name: Weighing_Balance_Title
data.value: The balance

data.name: Weighing_Balance_P1
data.value: A balance compares two things. Its beam rocks on a sharp knife edge, with a pan hanging from each end. Put equal masses in the pans and it rests level; add a little more to one side and that side sinks until the beam settles at a tilt. The pointer shows the tilt on a scale.

data.name: Weighing_Balance_P2
data.value: Why does it settle at all, instead of tipping right over? Because the beam's own centre of mass hangs a little below the knife edge. As the beam tilts, that centre swings out to one side and pulls the beam back, until the pulls balance. The closer the centre of mass is to the edge, the less it pulls back, and the farther a small difference tips the beam.

data.name: Weighing_Balance_Deeper
data.value: Here lies the balance-maker's dilemma. A centre of mass far below the edge makes a steady, quick beam that hardly notices a few grams. One very close makes a sensitive beam that swings slowly. And one above the edge makes a beam that tips over and stays tipped whatever is in the pans. Fine balances have a small screw on the pointer that moves the centre of mass up or down to set the sensitivity.

data.name: Weighing_Steelyard_P1
data.value: A balance needs a box of weights. A steelyard needs only one. Its arm hangs from a pivot near one end; the load hangs on a short arm on one side, and a single weight slides along the long arm on the other.

data.name: Weighing_Steelyard_P2
data.value: It is a lever. The arm balances when the load times its short distance equals the weight times its long distance. With the load five centimetres from the pivot and a one-kilogram weight, each five centimetres the weight slides out balances one more kilogram, so the arm can be marked in kilograms.

data.name: Weighing_Steelyard_Deeper
data.value: Steelyards were used for thousands of years in markets from China to Rome. Many have two hooks to hang from, one close to the load for heavy things and one farther away for light ones, each with its own row of marks. A small weight on a long arm can weigh a great deal, but every millimetre counts: a mark in the wrong place, or a weight filed a little lighter, cheats every customer.

data.name: Weighing_Spring_P1
data.value: A spring balance measures by stretching. Hang twice the load on a spring and it stretches twice as far; three times the load, three times as far. So a pointer on the spring's end can move along a scale marked in even steps.

data.name: Weighing_Spring_P2
data.value: Take the load off and the spring springs back to exactly where it started, as long as it was not stretched too far. Overload it, and its coils are bent for good: it stays a little longer, and from then on it reads too much, even with nothing on it.

data.name: Weighing_Spring_Deeper
data.value: Stretch in step with the pull is how most solid things behave when they are stretched only a little: the atoms are pulled slightly apart and pull back. Stretched too far they slide past each other into new places, and that is the lasting set. A good spring balance has a stop that will not let it be stretched past its limit, and a screw to set its pointer back to zero.

Slide it out to the far edge and it turns the arm harder, because it is farther from the post, and the scale reads too much; slide it in and it reads too little.

data.name: Weighing_Roberval_P2
data.value: Kitchen scales solve this with two parallel links, one above the other, joining the post to the pan's column, with a pin at every corner. The four pins make a parallelogram, so the column can only slide straight up and down, never tip. The links take the turning effect, and the spring under the column feels only the load's weight, wherever it sits.

data.name: Weighing_Roberval_Deeper
data.value: This linkage was worked out by a French mathematician in the 1600s and is still inside almost every pan scale: kitchen scales, shop scales, the scale under a supermarket checkout. Look at a letter scale or an old shop balance with its two pans on top: underneath, hidden in the base, are the same parallel links keeping the pans level.

data.name: Weighing_Strain_Title
data.value: The electronic scale

data.name: Weighing_Strain_P1
data.value: Inside an electronic scale there is no spring you could see stretch: there is a block of metal that bends very slightly under the load, far less than a hair's width. Glued to it is a strain gauge, a zigzag of thin metal foil. When the metal under it stretches, the foil stretches too, gets longer and thinner, and its electrical resistance rises a little.

data.name: Weighing_Strain_P2
data.value: The change is tiny, a fraction of an ohm, so it is measured in a bridge: four resistances in a ring, with the supply across one pair of corners and a sensitive meter across the other. Balanced, the meter reads nothing; the gauge's small change unbalances it by a few thousandths of a volt, and a chip turns that into kilograms on the display.

data.name: Weighing_Strain_Deeper
data.value: Warmth also changes a gauge's resistance, so one gauge on its own mistakes a warm room for a heavier load. Good load cells use four gauges, two on the top of the bar that are stretched and two underneath that are squeezed, as the four arms of the bridge. The bending pushes the bridge out of balance four times as hard as one gauge could, while warmth changes all four alike and cancels out.

data.name: Weighing_Moon_Title
data.value: Weighing on the Moon

data.name: Weighing_Moon_P1
data.value: A spring balance does not really measure how much stuff is in a bag; it measures how hard gravity pulls the bag down. Take it to the Moon, where gravity pulls about a sixth as hard, and the same bag stretches the spring a sixth as far: a spring marked on the Earth reads a sixth of the mass.

data.name: Weighing_Moon_P2
data.value: A balance compares the bag with known masses in the other pan. On the Moon both pans are pulled a sixth as hard, so they still balance at the same place. A balance reads the same on the Earth, the Moon or Mars: it measures mass, the amount of stuff, while a spring measures weight, the pull on it.

data.name: Weighing_Moon_Deeper
data.value: In everyday speech we say weight and mean mass, and on the Earth it makes no difference, because gravity is nearly the same everywhere on its surface. Not quite: it is about half a percent stronger at the poles than at the equator, so a sensitive electronic scale must be set for the place where it is used. A balance never needs that.
